clue.text: Move to London? Don't move south

parts.note: travelling to the capital is traditionally going up to London
to stick is to stay put

explanation.surface: Advice to someone thinking of relocating to the capital: stay where you are in the south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Move to London' looks like one phrase but splits: 'Move' is the definition and 'to London' gives UP. UP STICKS is British slang for leaving home to live somewhere else.
explanation.definitionFit: To up sticks is an idiom for relocating, packing up house and going elsewhere.

clue.text: He pairs off at start of evening as scribe's partner

indicators.note: off here means gone wrong or awry, so the letters of these words are scrambled
only the opening letter of the word evening is wanted here

explanation.surface: A man heads off in pairs early in the evening alongside a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges HE PAIRS into PHARISE, and 'at start of' adds the E from 'evening'. The Gospels repeatedly pair the scribes and Pharisees together.
explanation.definitionFit: In the New Testament the scribes and Pharisees are constantly named together, so a member of that Jewish sect is the scribe's companion.

clue.text: Business not strong, but one wants it to be green

definitions.text: one wants it to be green

parts.note: traffic is trade or dealing, as in drug traffic
light means weak or not heavy, as in a light beer

explanation.surface: A firm that is struggling, though someone hopes it will be environmentally friendly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'green' suggests eco-friendly business, but the motorist waiting at a junction is the one wanting green.
explanation.definitionFit: A driver waiting at a junction wants the signal to change to green so they can go.

clue.text: Caroller to be reprimanded around back of choir

indicators.note: the phrase for being told off goes around the other letter, holding it inside

parts.note: to catch it is an idiom for getting told off

indicators.note: only the final letter of the word choir is wanted

explanation.surface: A carol singer is due a telling-off for something at the rear of the choir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caroller' is not a singer but someone from Dickens's A Christmas Carol: Bob Cratchit, Scrooge's clerk. 'around' puts R, from 'back of choir', inside CATCH IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Bob Cratchit is a character in Dickens's A Christmas Carol, so in a playful sense he is one of the people of the Carol.

clue.text: Did exam problem, needing a healthy snack

parts.note: sat is the past tense of sitting an exam
a sum is an arithmetic problem

explanation.surface: Someone sat a tough exam paper and needed a nourishing bite afterwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A satsuma is a small citrus fruit, a typical wholesome thing to nibble between meals.

clue.text: Part of animal's leg it broke itself

indicators.note: broke signals that the letters of the following word are smashed and rearranged

explanation.surface: An animal's leg bone simply snapped of its own accord.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broke' rearranges the six letters of ITSELF; 'it' is just part of the surface sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: The stifle is the joint in a horse's or dog's hind leg corresponding to the human knee.

clue.text: Cow called: we heard its feelings

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound-alike, so a word that is pronounced the same is wanted

parts.note: a cow calling out mooed

explanation.surface: A cow lowed, and we listened to it expressing its emotions.
explanation.definitionFit: A mood is a state of mind or emotion, the feelings one has at a given time.

clue.text: Waiter and author go off together

parts.note: the pen stands for the writer, as in the pen is mightier
to elope is to run away together to marry

explanation.surface: A server in a restaurant and a writer run away with each other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waiter' suggests a restaurant, but it is Odysseus's wife in Homer, who waited twenty years for him to come home.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Odyssey, Odysseus's wife famously waits faithfully for twenty years for her husband's return.

clue.text: Tragic heroine's opponent lost

parts.note: someone anti something is opposed to it
something gone is lost or missing

explanation.surface: The heroine of a tragedy finds that her enemy has vanished.
explanation.definitionFit: The daughter of Oedipus is the title character of Sophocles' tragedy, who defies Creon to bury her brother.

clue.text: Holy book taken by a priest

parts.note: Lam is the abbreviation for Lamentations, a book of the Bible

explanation.surface: A clergyman picks up a sacred volume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken by' just joins the pieces: LAM sits before A.
explanation.definitionFit: A lama is a Tibetan Buddhist monk or spiritual teacher, a religious leader.

clue.text: In great shape to be orchestra leader?

explanation.surface: Someone is very fit, fit enough to lead an orchestra.
explanation.walkthrough: The orchestra's leader is the principal violinist, so being fit to serve as a fiddle is the comic second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means in excellent health, while read literally it is being suitable as the violin that leads an orchestra.

clue.text: At leisure before second plane trip, pop in here?

parts.note: free from duty, so off work and at leisure
a hop is a short flight

explanation.surface: Relaxing before your next flight, you might drop in at this airport store.
explanation.walkthrough: A hop is a short flight, so 'plane trip' gives HOP.
explanation.definitionFit: Travellers browse in the tax-free airport store before boarding, so it is a place to drop into briefly.

clue.text: Wodehouse hero in essence extremely slim

indicators.note: the first and last letters of slim are placed inside the word for essence

parts.note: the pith of something is its core or essence

indicators.note: extremely means at the extremes, so the first and last letters of slim are taken

explanation.surface: P.G. Wodehouse's hero is, at heart, very thin.
explanation.walkthrough: Psmith is a P.G. Wodehouse character who insists the P is silent. 'extremely' takes S and M, the first and last letters of 'slim'.
explanation.definitionFit: Psmith is the monocled, flamboyant protagonist of several P.G. Wodehouse novels, such as Leave It to Psmith.

clue.text: Set out to interrupt Chinese leader, so performed impressively

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into, so these letters go inside the leader's name

parts.note: Mao Zedong led the People's Republic of China

indicators.note: out signals that the letters of set are rearranged

explanation.surface: Laying out a challenge to the Chinese chairman, so the show went well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set out' reads as one phrase meaning arranged, but 'out' is the anagram signal giving EST, and 'to interrupt' marks the insertion. Maestoso is an Italian musical term.
explanation.definitionFit: Maestoso is a musical direction meaning to be played in a stately, majestic manner.

clue.text: Let down level in river

indicators.note: the word for level sits inside the river's name

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Scotland and in Wales
flat means level or even

explanation.surface: Water levels dropped in the river.
explanation.definitionFit: To deflate is to let the air out of something, as with a tyre.

clue.text: Popsy takes in short skirt — it's to get shorter

indicators.note: the word for an attractive woman holds the skirt inside it

parts.note: popsy and dish are both dated slang for an attractive woman
a mini is a very short skirt

explanation.surface: A glamorous young woman puts on a short skirt that shrinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Popsy' is dated British slang for an attractive young woman, as is DISH.
explanation.definitionFit: To diminish is to become smaller or less, so to reduce in length.

clue.text: Abundant academic employment

parts.note: prof is short for professor, a senior academic
use means employment, as in putting to use

explanation.surface: Plenty of jobs for university teachers.
explanation.definitionFit: Profuse means plentiful or lavish, existing in large quantities.

clue.text: Lets euro collapse without flinching

indicators.note: collapse signals that the letters of these words fall apart and are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone allows the single European currency to crash, unmoved.
explanation.definitionFit: Being resolute is being firm and determined, not shrinking back in the face of difficulty.

clue.text: Cartoon character Nietzsche created

explanation.surface: A comic-strip figure was invented by a German philosopher.
explanation.walkthrough: The comic-book hero shares his name with the English rendering of Nietzsche's Ubermensch, the ideal superior human.
explanation.definitionFit: The comic hero from Krypton is one sense; the other is Nietzsche's concept of the higher human being, usually translated with this word.

clue.text: Early workers take in four's little lad

indicators.note: the insects hold the boy's name inside them

parts.note: worker bees, so bees are workers
Tiny Tim is the young son of Bob Cratchit, the answer to 4 down

explanation.surface: Employees start early to welcome a small boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'four' refers to clue 4 down: Tiny Tim is the little son of Bob Cratchit in A Christmas Carol.
explanation.definitionFit: Betimes is an old word for in good time, at an early hour.

clue.text: Propose to plant virtually wild tree

indicators.note: planting puts one thing into another, so the trimmed word goes inside

parts.note: to move a motion is to propose it

indicators.note: virtually means almost, so the word for wild is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: wild means furious or angry

explanation.surface: A suggestion to put an untamed tree in the ground, more or less.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant' looks like a noun beside 'tree', but 'to plant' is the insertion signal; 'virtually' (almost) drops the final letter of ANGRY to leave ANGR.
explanation.definitionFit: Mangroves are trees that grow in tidal coastal swamps in the tropics.

clue.text: Ejection of man in tournament, not the leader

indicators.note: not the leader means the first letter of the word is removed

parts.note: a jouster competes at a medieval tournament

explanation.surface: A knight is thrown out of a tournament, though he is not the frontrunner.
explanation.definitionFit: An ouster is a removal or expulsion, chiefly in American legal and political usage.

clue.text: Plain measure of speech

indicators.note: in speech, so the word as said aloud is wanted, matching a different spelling

parts.note: a step is a measure, as in taking steps

explanation.surface: A simple yardstick for how someone talks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain' looks like an adjective (simple), but it is the noun: a flat grassland.
explanation.definitionFit: A steppe is a vast treeless grassy plain, as in Russia and Central Asia.

clue.text: PM protects town

parts.note: Lord North was British prime minister during the American War of Independence
shields means protects or guards

explanation.surface: The prime minister defends a place.
explanation.walkthrough: NORTH SHIELDS is a town on the River Tyne in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: North Shields is a town in Tyneside, England.

clue.text: Salesman pockets a cut

indicators.note: pockets means puts inside, so the letter goes into the salesman's word

parts.note: rep is short for sales representative

explanation.surface: A sales representative skims off a share.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' looks like a slice of the money, but it is the verb: to cut a crop.
explanation.definitionFit: To reap is to harvest a crop by cutting it.

clue.text: Power to smell, a feature of camel

indicators.note: to means added onto, so the power letter is attached to the end

parts.note: hum is British slang for a bad smell
P is the symbol for power in physics

explanation.surface: A camel's nose is so keen it could be called a special trait.
explanation.walkthrough: HUM is British slang for a bad smell.
explanation.definitionFit: A camel stores fat in the lump on its back, its most distinctive physical trait.

clue.text: Run wild, with marked energy

parts.note: stamped means marked with a stamp
E is the symbol for energy in physics

explanation.surface: A frenzied rush, with obvious vigour.
explanation.definitionFit: To stampede is for a herd to flee in panic, rushing about uncontrollably.

clue.text: Raising a dust? That's not very specific

explanation.surface: Kicking up a fuss is too vague a description.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is literal: brushing a floor raises dust.
explanation.definitionFit: Using a broom stirs up dust; and a broad generalisation covers everything without detail.
